title: Though the fig tree (Habakkuk 3:17–19)
hook: no fruit, no flock, and yet I will rejoice

segments.voice: Yesterday, little Bethlehem, the hillside village Micah pointed to. Your line was the least of the towns. Who was the overlooked person you thanked? Day four hundred ninety-one.

Most books of the prophets have the prophet talking to the people for God. Habakkuk is different. Habakkuk talks back to God. His book opens with a complaint, in the King James Bible: "O LORD, how long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear!" Violence everywhere, he says, the law ignored, the wicked winning. And God's answer makes it worse: the Babylonians are coming, a fierce army that will sweep through like the desert wind. So Habakkuk climbs a watchtower, in his words, to wait and see what God will say next. Three short chapters later, he comes down singing. Today is the song.

The song's ending is one of the most honest passages in the Bible. Habakkuk imagines the worst. In the King James: "Although the fig tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vines; the labour of the olive shall fail, and the fields shall yield no meat; the flock shall be cut off from the fold, and there shall be no herd in the stalls." Count it. Figs, grapes, olives, grain, sheep, cattle. For a farming people, that's everything. The pantry, the bank account, the retirement plan. All of it gone. And then one small word: "Yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation." Yet. Habakkuk doesn't say things will turn out fine. He doesn't say the fig tree will bloom after all. He says even if it doesn't. His joy is anchored somewhere the harvest can't reach. Then the last picture: "he will make my feet like hinds' feet." A hind is a female deer, and in those hills deer pick their way up steep, rocky slopes without falling. The ground doesn't get easier. The feet get surer. And the book ends with a note for the choir leader, about stringed instruments, which means this cry of faith from the edge of disaster was meant to be sung together. Christians in hard seasons have leaned on these verses for centuries, in famines, prisons and hospital rooms. Some churches read Habakkuk as a pattern for honest prayer: complain first, wait on the watchtower, then sing. The yet doesn't cancel the complaint. It comes after it.
screen: `NOT IF IT BLOOMS. EVEN IF IT DOESN'T.`
`FEET LIKE A DEER'S ON THE ROCKS.`
then, large: `YET I WILL REJOICE IN THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rejoice in one thing on a bad day. Settle, and breathe. If today is hard, let it be hard. Name what's not blooming: money, health, a relationship, plans that fell apart. Say it plainly, the way Habakkuk listed his empty fields. Don't rush past it. Then look for one thing, just one, that's still good: a person who loves you, a breath that comes easily, light through a window, a song you know by heart. Rest your attention there. If you pray, you can say Habakkuk's yet in your own heart. If you don't, simply let that one good thing be enough for now. The bell holds the time.
Though the fig tree. Habakkuk's song from the edge of disaster: even if every harvest fails, yet I will rejoice.
Your line: yet I will rejoice. Today, when something fails or falls through, finish the sentence out loud: and yet. Then name one good thing. Day four hundred ninety-one.

screen: `DAY 491 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: HE WILL SING OVER YOU.`

howItsDone: Many Christians turn to Habakkuk 3:17–18 in times of loss, and its words have been set in hymns and songs; Habakkuk 2:4, on the just living by faith, is quoted three times in the New Testament.

myth: Habakkuk says the fig tree will bloom again
he never promises that. he says even if it doesn't, yet I will rejoice.
Habakkuk complains to God out loud
his book opens with "O LORD, how long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear!"
the song was meant to be sung
it ends with a note for the chief singer, on stringed instruments.

fork.setup: you're a farmer. the figs didn't blossom, the olives failed, the sheep are gone. what does Habakkuk do?
options: name it all, and rejoice anyway.
fork.reveal: he lists every loss honestly, and then says "yet I will rejoice in the LORD." the yet comes after the complaint, not instead of it.

original.note: Hebrew: but I, yet I. the first word of Habakkuk 3:18, the turn of the whole song.

trapdoor: what you thought: a cheerful verse about staying positive.
what it means: a prophet names total loss honestly, every crop and every flock, and still chooses joy in God.
what a scholar hears: the book moves from complaint to watchtower to song, and ends with a note for the choir leader, so it was meant for worship.

notes: Habakkuk 2:4 is quoted in Romans 1:17, Galatians 3:11 and Hebrews 10:38 ('three times'). Confirm.
'Fields shall yield no meat': 'meat' means food/grain in the KJV; rendered as grain in the count. Confirm.
Habakkuk 3:19's closing note 'To the chief singer on my stringed instruments' paraphrased as a note for the choir leader.
Original: וַאֲנִי opens 3:18 in the Masoretic text. Confirm pointing.
'Leaned on these verses for centuries, in famines, prisons and hospital rooms' is general and unsourced; soften if needed.
